common_name: Blaze Little Bluestem (Vivid Red-Orange Fall-Color Native Grass)

planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Blaze was originally selected in Nebraska for pasture use and has since become popular for its exceptionally intense fall color.

directions: Plant Blaze little bluestem in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, where it forms an erect, broom-shaped clump of narrow blue-green leaves. Originally selected in 1967 as a high-performing Nebraska pasture grass, it earned a second life in gardens for foliage that shifts through pink-orange and reddish-purple before erupting into an especially vivid blaze of orange-red fall color that persists well into winter. Fluffy, silvery-white seed heads rise above the foliage in late summer and provide food for songbirds through the cold months. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Ha Ha Tonka Little Bluestem (Fuzzy Blue-Green Native Grass, PP32,374)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this patented selection was seed-collected at Ha Ha Tonka State Park in Missouri and refined through years of trialing by plantsmen Cassian Schmidt and Piet Oudolf.

directions: Grow Ha Ha Tonka little bluestem in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun for its best upright form. The blue-green blades are covered in fine, dense hairs that catch afternoon light and create a soft, glowing halo effect around the clump, deepening through late summer into streaks of red-orange and gray as the season turns. It grows a bit taller and more vigorously than many little bluestem selections, forming a substantial architectural presence at the middle or back of a native planting. Shear the clump to a few inches above the crown in late winter before new shoots emerge.

common_name: Chameleon Little Bluestem (Variegated White-Striped Native Grass, PP31,339)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Chameleon arose as a chance variegated seedling in a French trial field and is propagated only by division to preserve its striped leaves.

directions: Site Chameleon little bluestem in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to keep its compact, tidy habit and best coloring. Unlike the solid blue-green of typical little bluestem, its narrow blades are boldly striped in white and green through spring and summer, then take on washes of pink and light purple as cooler weather arrives in fall. This smaller-statured selection is well suited to container culture, small-space gardens, or as a bright textural accent at the front of a border. Cut back to a few inches in late winter before new growth begins.

common_name: Blue Paradise Little Bluestem (Powder-Blue Native Grass, PP28,145)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Paradise was selected and propagated by culm division for its intensely powder-blue summer foliage.

directions: Grow Blue Paradise little bluestem in lean, well-drained soil in full sun for its most saturated color. Its defining feature is unusually vivid, powder-blue summer foliage that stands out even among other blue-toned little bluestem selections, transitioning to deep wine-purple and burgundy tones as nights cool in autumn. Airy, silver-fringed seed heads appear above the foliage in late summer and hold through winter for texture and bird interest. Cut the clump back hard in late winter before new growth resumes each spring.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Karl's Cousin Big Bluestem (Tight Upright Architectural Native Prairie Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun; Karl's Cousin was found growing wild in western Michigan and selected for an unusually tight, non-flopping habit.

directions: Plant Karl's Cousin big bluestem in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun, where it tolerates heat, humidity, and drought once established. Discovered as a naturally occurring wild selection in Michigan, it forms a notably tight, upright, architectural clump that resists the floppy, open habit common in big bluestem, drawing comparisons to the stiff verticality of Karl Foerster feather reed grass. Blue-green basal foliage shifts to shades of purple-blue through the season, capped by the turkey-foot seed heads typical of the species in late summer and fall. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges.
scientific_name_note: Marketed under the trademark name Karl's Cousin; registered cultivar name is 'Nondhwr'.

common_name: Black Mountain Splitbeard Bluestem (Compact Glaucous Blue-Green Native Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring on sandy, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Black Mountain was selected by North Carolina Arboretum curator Terry Dalton for a more refined, compact habit than the wild species.

directions: Plant Black Mountain splitbeard bluestem in sandy, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun, following the lean-soil preferences of the wild species. This selection keeps the glaucous, blue-green basal foliage of splitbeard bluestem but stays noticeably shorter and more compact than typical plants, making it easier to place in smaller native gardens and border edges. In fall, paired flowering stalks open into the signature forked, silvery-white seed heads that give the species its common name, contrasting nicely against warm bronze foliage tones. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Morning Mist Prairie Dropseed (Upright Red-Culmed Native Grass, PP14,344)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Morning Mist is slow to establish in its first year or two, like other prairie dropseed selections, before its deep root system matures.

directions: Plant Morning Mist prairie dropseed in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun, where its extensive root system eventually makes it highly drought-tolerant. This patented selection produces an unusually high number of sturdy, upright, red-tinted flowering stems that hold at a uniform height above dense, gently arching, fine-textured foliage, giving a tidier and more consistent silhouette than the straight species. The airy, reddish-brown flower panicles carry the same distinctive fragrance, often likened to coriander or warm popcorn, that prairie dropseed is known for. Foliage turns a rich golden yellow in fall; cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes
